title: U.S. House · Texas's 8th District
area: A redrawn district in southeast Texas covering parts of Montgomery, Walker, San Jacinto and surrounding counties north of Houston.

context.text: Open seat: incumbent Morgan Luttrell (R) retired from public office rather than seek re-election after Texas redrew its congressional district boundaries in August 2025. Laura Jones won the March 3, 2026 Democratic primary over Keith Coleman after having previously run for this seat in 2020, 2022 and 2024, losing each time. Jessica Steinmann won a multi-candidate Republican primary.

candidates.name: Laura Jones
candidates.ballotNote: Won the March 3, 2026 Democratic primary over Keith Coleman, 65.7% to 34.3%

summary.text: Laura Jones is the Democratic nominee for the open U.S. House seat in Texas's 8th District. Born in Houston, she worked as a business professional and real estate sales agent, and describes herself as a small business owner and Army mom. She has sought this seat in each cycle since 2020, losing the 2020 Democratic primary and the 2022 and 2024 general elections to Republican Morgan Luttrell, and is running on affordability, a higher minimum wage, and Medicare for All.

background.text: Born in Houston, Texas. In a 2020 Ballotpedia survey she described herself as a native Texan, wife, mother and business professional who was born and raised in Houston, raised six children with her husband, and operated a business.
Her Ballotpedia profile lists her career experience as a business professional and a real estate sales agent with HomePlus Realty Group.

In 2020 she said she had served for a year as chair of the San Jacinto County Democrats and as field director for Texas Senate District 3 under the Texas Democratic Party's Non-Urban Rural Caucus, and that she and her husband had moved to a rural East Texas town.
Describes herself on her campaign website as a lifelong Texan, Army mom, small business owner, and working-class American.
Ran for Texas's 8th Congressional District in 2020 and lost the Democratic primary to Elizabeth Hernandez.
Won the Democratic nomination in 2022 and lost the general election to Republican Morgan Luttrell, 68.1% to 30.5%.
Won the Democratic nomination again in 2024 and lost the general election to incumbent Luttrell, 68.2% to 31.8%.
Won the March 3, 2026 Democratic primary over Keith Coleman, 65.7% to 34.3%, after Texas redrew the district and Luttrell chose not to seek re-election.

priorities.text: Affordability and a living wage: raise the minimum wage and tie it to the cost of living so that a full-time worker can afford housing, utilities and food.
Expand and improve Medicare for All, arguing it is the only way to guarantee healthcare access and bring down costs.
Lower taxes for the '99%' by making billionaires and large corporations 'pay what they owe.'

positions.summary: Says the federal minimum wage has been stagnant since 2009 and should be raised and tied to the cost of living.
Supports expanding and improving Medicare for All, saying healthcare is a right rather than a privilege tied to employment.
Says billionaires and large corporations should pay more so taxes can be lowered for working families.

candidates.researchNotes: Laura Jones's education and employment history beyond what appears on Ballotpedia and her campaign website were not found.

candidates.name: Jessica Steinmann
candidates.ballotNote: Won the March 3, 2026 Republican primary over five other candidates

summary.text: Jessica Steinmann is the Republican nominee for the open U.S. House seat in Texas's 8th District. An attorney, she served as Director of the Justice Department's Office for Victims of Crime from 2020 to 2021 and later as Executive General Counsel at the America First Policy Institute, and describes herself as an 'America First conservative.' She won the March 3, 2026 Republican primary with 68.0% of the vote.

background.text: According to her campaign website, she was born and went to high school in Harris County, just outside the district.
Earned a bachelor's degree from the University of Texas at Austin and a J.D. from Baylor University.
Says she previously served in the office of U.S. Senator Ted Cruz, and that she helped draft Texas's election integrity law.

Served as Director of the Office for Victims of Crime in the U.S. Department of Justice from 2020 to 2021; says she oversaw nearly $9 billion and awarded over $2.5 billion in 2020 funding to crime victims, including the largest federal funding to combat domestic human trafficking.

After leaving the Trump administration, worked as Executive General Counsel at the America First Policy Institute, where she says she led litigation including a lawsuit representing 36 U.S. Air Force members against the Biden administration's COVID-19 vaccine mandate and a lawsuit on behalf of high school track athletes over transgender participation in girls' sports.

Says she led Republican women's groups and served as a Texas Committeewoman on the RNC Platform Committee; previously served as president of The Woodlands Republican Women and on the Montgomery County Child Welfare Board.
Won the March 3, 2026 Republican primary in a six-candidate field with 68.0% of the vote.

Describes herself as a wife and mother of two sons; her campaign website says she and her husband Brandon, the elected Montgomery County Clerk, live in Montgomery County, and that she is a member of the Conroe Noon Lions Club, The Woodlands Rotary and the Federalist Society.

priorities.text: Secure the southern border: finish the border wall, end 'catch-and-release,' and reduce illegal immigration.
'Protect children and families': campaign material says she will oppose gender-identity curricula in schools and defend parental rights over children's upbringing.
Combat human trafficking, citing her DOJ record directing federal anti-trafficking funding.

positions.summary: Says she will fight to finish the border wall, end 'catch-and-release,' and restore 'law and order' at the southern border.
positions.quote: I will fight to finish President Trump's wall, end catch-and-release, and restore law and order at our southern border.

candidates.researchNotes: Steinmann's biography is drawn from her campaign website and Ballotpedia; claims about her professional work are her own descriptions and were not independently verified.
